Live view

How endoscopy works

Follow the scope.

An endoscope is a soft tube as thin as a finger, with a light and a camera at its tip. Scroll to follow its path. Dr Muguti sees the lining on screen in real time, takes tiny samples and treats many problems without a single cut.

01Gastroscopy · upper gut

The food pipe

The scope passes gently over the tongue and down the oesophagus. You breathe normally throughout. This is where reflux damage, narrowing and swallowing problems are found.

HeartburnFood stickingBarrett's checks

02Gastroscopy

The stomach

A little air opens the stomach so every fold can be seen. Ulcers, inflammation and bleeding points show up clearly. Bleeding can often be stopped there and then.

UlcersBleedingBiopsy

03Gastroscopy · complete

The duodenum

The first part of the small bowel. Samples taken here help diagnose coeliac disease and other causes of anaemia. The whole upper check usually takes 5 to 15 minutes.

AnaemiaCoeliac checksHome same day

04Colonoscopy · lower gut

The rectum

For a colonoscopy you are sedated and comfortable. The scope enters from below, where piles, fissures and causes of bleeding are checked first.

BleedingPilesChange in habit

05Colonoscopy

The colon

The scope travels the full length of the large bowel. Polyps, small growths that can turn into cancer over years, are lifted off painlessly during the same test.

Polyp removalCancer screening

06Colonoscopy · complete

The caecum

The start of the large bowel, and the end of the journey. You hear what was found before you go home, in plain words, with photos where useful.

Results explainedReport to your doctor

Profile

OverviewClinical workTeaching & researchPublic serviceCareer

Biography

Dr Edwin Gamba Muguti is a specialist consultant surgeon, a university lecturer in surgery and a former Deputy Minister of Health. He has served patients in Zimbabwe for more than four decades.

He leads The Endoscopy Suite & Surgical Clinic in Belvedere, Harare, where he examines the digestive tract with a camera, operates through keyhole incisions wherever it is safe, and manages complex gastrointestinal problems. He sees every patient himself, from first consultation to follow-up.

Clinical work

  • EndoscopyGastroscopy and colonoscopy with real-time video imaging, biopsies and polyp removal.
  • Keyhole (laparoscopic) surgeryAppendix and gallbladder removal, hernia repair and surgery for acid reflux.
  • Gastrointestinal and liver careConditions of the bile ducts, liver, oesophagus and bowel.
  • Breast and cancer surgerySurgery for breast cancer and other tumours, and repair of soft tissue.
  • Trauma and emergenciesAbdominal and chest injuries, stab and gunshot wounds, and acute appendicitis.

Teaching and research

Dr Muguti has been a Senior Lecturer in the Department of Surgery at the University of Zimbabwe College of Health Sciences since 1999, training the next generation of doctors and surgeons. He has published peer-reviewed research on:

  • Breast cancerMaking palliative radiotherapy work better for women with breast cancer that has spread.
  • Surgical safetyTesting risk scores such as POSSUM, which predict how likely complications are after an operation.
  • Emergency surgeryTreating penetrating injuries that cross the chest and abdomen, and necrotising fasciitis, a fast-spreading infection under the skin.

Public service

From 2005 to 2009 Dr Muguti served as Deputy Minister of Health and Child Welfare, working on national public-health programmes, the distribution of medical resources and oversight of clinical services. He also served as a Member of Parliament.

Your visit

From first message to follow-up.

  1. Book

    Pick an open time online, or message us on WhatsApp. A referral letter helps but isn't required.

  2. Consultation

    Dr Muguti listens, examines you and explains your options before anything is booked.

  3. Preparation

    You get written instructions and your own preparation timetable.

  4. Procedure day

    Arrive early with an adult to take you home. We check consent and answer last questions.

  5. Recovery

    You rest while the team monitors you, then hear what was found in plain words.

  6. Follow-up

    Biopsy results and next steps are discussed with you and shared with your doctor.

Why there are no patient reviews here. Zimbabwe's rules for medical practitioners do not allow advertising with patient testimonials. Instead, this site shows you exactly what to expect, so you can judge for yourself.
